title: Partisan media, untrustworthy news sites, and political misperceptions
screen_reason: Primary aim is the association between website exposure and political misperceptions (a belief study, which alone would be excluded), BUT the Measures section reports descriptive behavioural exposure to a 668-site untrustworthy-domain list from browser-history data for 671 US adults: a verbatim mean of 1.19 visits per respondent over 90 days (EXPOSURE intensity). That descriptive statistic is a genuine behavioural exposure estimate with a denominator, so the paper is included under the rule that a study whose aim is something else still counts if a descriptive share/intensity is reported anywhere.

estimates.platform: Desktop web browsing (Google Chrome history, all domains)
estimates.date: 90 days of browsing preceding each survey; visit records begin between 28 December 2017 and 30 January 2018 and end on the participant's survey start date (survey fielded 28 March - 30 April 2018)
estimates.measure_type: Mean number of visits per respondent to untrustworthy websites in the 90 days before the survey (behavioural browser-history data)
estimates.value_raw: M = 1.19 visits per respondent (SD = 3.60), range 0-49; 60.8% of respondents visited zero untrustworthy sites and 95.6% visited four or fewer
estimates.denominator: 671 American adult Facebook users who completed the survey and uploaded acceptable 90-day browsing histories (Facebook-ad convenience sample, Web Historian Chrome extension)
estimates.definition: A recorded browser visit to any of the 668 websites on the Allcott, Gentzkow and Yu (2019) list of untrustworthy sites; visits counted as unique URLs at the day level over the 90-day window (four sites - dailywire, ijr, dailycaller, wnd - were moved to the partisan-media list instead)
estimates.misinfo_def: "Untrustworthy sites are not driven by journalistic values of accuracy, accountability, and verification, but instead provide content that is false or misleading (Guess et al., 2020b)."
estimates.source_quote: were very rare; 60.8% of respondents visited zero sites and 95.6% visited four or less. The mean number of visits across respondents was 1.19 (SD = 3.60) and the range was from 0 to 49 sites visited.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Exposure defined by domain membership on Allcott et al.'s (2019) 668-site untrustworthy list, described as 'the most expansive to date', itself built by combining five existing lists compiled by researchers, journalists and fact-checking sites. No item-level verification of the content actually seen; no inter-coder reliability applicable.
estimates.moderator_quote: Our measure of untrustworthy website exposure was calculated using a list of 668 untrustworthy websites created by Allcott et al., (2019). Their list, which is the most expansive to date, was created by combining five existing lists of untrustworthy sites previously gathered by researchers, journalists, and fact-checking sites (see Supplemental Information for list). We used the browsing data to examine how frequently respondents visited these sites in the 90 days before taking the survey.
estimates.notes: Judgement calls. (1) The sentence mixes units - 'mean number of visits' but 'range was from 0 to 49 sites visited' - so 1.19 is most plausibly mean day-level unique URLs on untrustworthy domains per respondent over 90 days (the construction stated for the partisan variables in note 7), but the paper is not fully explicit. (2) Denominator: descriptives are reported for the analytic sample of 671 (the regressions drop to N = 589 because of missing party ID); I use 671. (3) Recruitment was a Facebook-ad convenience sample (74.5% women, 78.7% White, well-educated), so this is NOT a population-representative exposure rate; sampling_frame is coded panel_trace because the estimate itself comes from browser-trace data. (4) Desktop Chrome only - the authors explicitly note they cannot capture mobile, TV, chat apps or in-app social media browsing, so this understates total exposure.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, and the main thing an adjudicator should look at: '60.8% of respondents visited zero sites' (untrustworthy). Its complement, 39.2% visiting at least one untrustworthy site in 90 days, would be a clean REACH estimate, but R8 explicitly bars a complement I compute (100 - 60.8), and the paper never states the at-least-once share. I therefore created no REACH row, and did not create a row carrying 60.8 either, because a 60.8 value would invert the sign of the construct if pooled. If the review's rule allows the complement of a verbatim zero-exposure share, this paper yields REACH = 39.2% of 671 US adults over 90 days, source-level, domain_list ground truth. Also not extracted: (a) '95.6% visited four or less' - a cumulative distribution point, not a misinformation prevalence; (b) zero-visit shares for partisan/centrist sites (18.2% liberal, 44.1% conservative, 8.2% centrist) and their visit means (Liberal M = 38.28; Centrist M = 74.73; Conservative M = 7.98) - partisan slant is not a veracity judgement, so these are not misinformation exposure; (c) all six OLS regressions predicting belief accuracy - belief/misperception outcomes are explicitly out of scope; (d) figures cited from other papers (e.g. Guess et al.) are barred by R8.

rob.design: Cross-sectional survey linked to donated web-browsing traces. Recruitment by Facebook advertisement to US adults, March-April 2018: ads shown in the right-hand column of 266,827 Facebook users' pages, 3,735 clicked (1.4% click-through), 764 completed the survey, 736 uploaded browsing data, 65 removed for insufficient data (<7 days of browsing or <2,000 site-visit records), leaving 671 with both; regression models N = 589. Explicitly a convenience, non-probability sample (74.5% women, 78.7% White, median education a 4-year degree, 48 states + DC). Browsing captured by Web Historian, an open-source Chrome extension collecting the previous 90 days of history with informed consent (>15 million visits; median participant visited 432 domains). Untrustworthy exposure operationalised by membership in Allcott et al.'s (2019) 668-domain list; partisan slant from Eady et al.'s (2019) IRT scores for 140 outlets (validated against DW-NOMINATE, r = .93). Belief accuracy self-reported on a 5-point scale for six claims whose truth status was set by the researchers 'in accordance with the best available evidence produced by journalists, fact-checkers, and related experts'. No inter-coder reliability reported (classification is list-based); desktop-only measurement is the acknowledged main limitation; analyses are cross-sectional, so no causal claim.
rob.item6_quote: Untrustworthy sites are not driven by journalistic values of accuracy, accountability, and verification, but instead provide content that is false or misleading (Guess et al., 2020b).
rob.item10_quote: Consistent with prior research (Guess et al., 2020b), visits to these untrustworthy websites were very rare; 60.8% of respondents visited zero sites and 95.6% visited four or less. The mean number of visits across respondents was 1.19 (SD = 3.60) and the range was from 0 to 49 sites visited.
